title: Plant traits explain variation in symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses to global nitrogen enrichment: a meta-analysis

paper_content.abstract: Anthropogenic nitrogen enrichment is widely expected to suppress symbiotic nitrogen fixation in terrestrial ecosystems. Nevertheless, observed symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses remain incompletely explained by exogenous nitrogen inputs, climate, and edaphic factors. In this meta-analysis, we integrate 908 globally distributed field measurements to identify the key predictors that improve simulation of symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses to nitrogen enrichment. On average, symbiotic nitrogen fixation declines by 33.0% upon nitrogen enrichment, with the reduction being more pronounced in non-croplands than croplands. Models considering only environmental factors overestimate symbiotic nitrogen fixation decline relative to observations. The better performance of plant traits like plant growth and biomass allocation (shoot:root ratio) partially buffers symbiotic nitrogen fixation suppression under nitrogen enrichment. Integrating both environmental factors and plant performance traits improves predictive accuracy of symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses by 42.7% and brings the simulated symbiotic nitrogen fixation reductions into close agreement with observations. The alterations in plant performance traits are thus critical for explaining variability in terrestrial symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses, and incorporating plant trait dynamics in Earth System Models can quantitatively partition the compensatory symbiotic nitrogen fixation supported by nitrogen-fixing plant growth from the direct negative impact of nitrogen inputs.
paper_content.introduction:
Symbiotic nitrogen (N) fixation (SNF), carried out by plant-microbe symbionts (e.g., rhizobia and Frankia), sustains critical terrestrial ecosystem functions, including biogeochemical N cycling and gross primary production1,2. Globally, SNF replenishes 50-70 Tg N yr−1 in croplands3,4 and 31-66 Tg N yr−1 in non-croplands1,4. Anthropogenic N enrichment, especially via atmospheric deposition and synthetic fertilizer inputs, has markedly altered SNF dynamics5,6. Consistent with carbon-economic theory, the declines in SNF under exogenous N sufficiency are confirmed, particularly for facultative fixers7,8. Yet the observed magnitude of N-induced SNF suppression remains poorly predicted by environmental factors alone9. In particular, substantial taxon-specific variation persists under comparable conditions10–12, implicating unaccounted plant traits (e.g., performance traits) as key regulators. However, the role of plant performance traits in predicting SNF responses to N enrichment remains largely overlooked, particularly at large spatial scales.

A comprehensive understanding of SNF responses and their predictors is essential to project terrestrial N budgets accurately, thus informing ecosystem functionality assessments under anthropogenic change.

Environmental factors, including exogenous N inputs, climate, and edaphic conditions, have been extensively investigated for their roles in regulationg SNF responses9,13. Carbon-economic theory posits that exogenous N inputs (e.g., nitrate and ammonium enrichment) suppress legume SNF, as direct N uptake is energetically cheaper than maintaining N-fixing symbionts14,15. Accordingly, legumes in N-rich conditions preferentially assimilate soil bioavailable N while down-regulating SNF16,17, thereby weakening plant-microbe mutualism under N enrichment18. This suppression operates mechanistically through reduced rhizobia colonization, diminished rhizobia populations, and curtailed nodule biomass17,19,20. Climatic and edaphic factors can also modulate SNF sensitivity to N enrichment. For instance, SNF declines upon N enrichment were less pronounced at high mean annual temperatures9, while elevated soil carbon: N ratios and pH buffer diazotrophs against N inhibition13 and consequently attenuate SNF declines. Despite the importance of environmental factors, these factors explain only 2-33% of observed variation in SNF responses upon N enrichment9,13, leaving a large proportion of variability attributable to unidentified predictors.

Plant performance traits emerge as critical predictors of SNF responses to environmental change. Biomass allocation patterns substantially contribute to observed SNF variability21, e.g., in Glycine max, SNF increases by 35% as shoot biomass rises from 842.9 g m−2 to 1200.2 g m−2 22, while root biomass consistently correlates with SNF magnitude21. Higher shoot:root ratios often correlate with enhanced SNF, potentially through improved light interception, as light availability is a key factor regulating the symbiotic efficiency of legumes23,24. Given that N enrichment frequently enhances biomass accumulation and shoot:root ratios in N-fixing plants25–27, these trait adjustments may partially alleviate SNF declines by augmenting photosynthetic capacity and carbon supply to fuel energetically costly N fixation. Accordingly, we hypothesized that plant trait plasticity may explain a significant fraction of the residual heterogeneity in SNF responses to N enrichment (Hypothesis 1). Critically, the quantitative global-scale contribution of plant performance traits to SNF responses, beyond environmental predictors, has yet to be assessed.

Divergent baseline N conditions between non-croplands and croplands due to long-term anthropogenic management can fundamentally alter SNF responses to experimental N enrichment. Chronic fertilization in croplands elevates soil N availability while simultaneously disrupting legume-rhizobia mutualism and reshaping microbial communities28,29. Consequently, legumes in croplands may acclimatize to high exogenous N inputs and exhibit attenuated SNF sensitivity relative to non-croplands18,30,31. In contrast, N-fixing plants in non-croplands experience more marked declines in nodule biomass and SNF following N inputs due to limited microbial adaptation, abrupt symbiosis breakdown, and competitive exclusion pressure from non-fixing species7,32,33. Accordingly, we propose that N enrichment suppresses SNF more markedly in non-croplands than croplands (Hypothesis 2).

This study focuses on accurate SNF predictability rather than mechanistic causation, to identify plant predictors explaining heterogeneity in SNF responses to N enrichment across sites and taxa. Leveraging a global synthesis based on 908 field observations, we determine the dominant predictors of SNF responses to N enrichment. Two specific questions were addressed: (a) What proportion of variability in SNF responses is explained by environmental factors (exogenous N inputs, climate, and edaphic properties) versus plant performance traits? (b) What are the differences in SNF responses between croplands and non-croplands?
paper_content.results:
Environmental forces are insufficient to explain SNF responses upon N enrichment

N enrichment reduced SNF (8.49 g N m−2 yr−1 of SNF upon N enrichment versus 9.51 g N m−2 yr−1 upon ambient conditions), partially attributable to decreased SNF per unit biomass (Fig. S1). On average, the weighted effect size of SNF was −0.40 (95% CI: –0.58 ~ −0.22), corresponding to a 33.0% global decline relative to controls (Fig. 1a). This suppression in SNF intensified poleward (slope = −0.01, p < 0.05) (Fig. S2), and SNF decline was aggravated with high levels of N enrichment rate (a slope of −0.16, p < 0.01) (Fig. 1b).

Environmental factors partially accounted for the global variation in SNF responses to N enrichment (Fig. S3). SNF decline attenuated in conditions with higher mean annual temperature (slope = 0.42, p < 0.05), while the effects of precipitation on SNF response were insignificant (p = 0.50; Fig. S3a, b). Edaphically, SNF decline amplified under lower soil pH (slope = 0.21, p < 0.05), greater carbon:N ratio (slope = −0.53, p < 0.05), and elevated available phosphorus (slope = −0.32, p < 0.05). Ambient soil ammonium (p = 0.17) and nitrate (p = 0.66) exerted negligible influences (Fig. S3c–g). Moreover, SNF decline was more pronounced in soils with higher microbial biomass carbon (slope = −0.33, p < 0.05) and microbial biomass N (slope = −0.41, p < 0.05) (Fig. S3h–i). Notably, N enrichment rate (relative importance = 37.4%) and soil carbon:N ratio (relative importance = 31.4%) emerged as dominant predictors of the variability of SNF responses at a global scale (Fig. 1). The combined factors (i.e., mean annual temperature, N enrichment rate, pH, soil carbon:N ratio, available phosphorus, the carbon and N contents in microbial biomass) explained approximately one third of the variability of SNF responses at a global scale (34.2%) (Fig. 1c).

Enhancement of plant performance traits ameliorated the SNF decline upon N enrichment

SNF response to N enrichment also diverged across plant taxa (ranging from −1.29 to 0.44; Fig. 2a). Plant trait plasticity buffers SNF declines upon N enrichment. The enhanced N-fixing plant biomass or shoot:root ratios upon N enrichment attenuated SNF decline, while changes in plant nutrient contents had little impact on SNF responses (Fig. 2). Specifically, SNF decline trended to neutralize with the enhancement of plant performance traits, with a slope of 0.47 for N-fixing plant biomass (p < 0.001) and 2.75 for the plant shoot:root ratios (p < 0.01), respectively (Fig. 2).

Integrating plant performance traits, soil properties, microbial traits, N enrichment rate, and climatic factors explained 48.8% of the variability in SNF responses to N enrichment (Fig. 3). This represents a substantial improvement of 42.7% (a relative increase in explanatory power) over the prediction considering merely environmental factors (34.2% explained variance in Fig. 1c), which was consistently confirmed by both linear mixed-effects model and structural equation model (SEM). In the SEM, soil carbon:N ratio was the crucial driver of the variability in SNF responses to N enrichment (relative importance = 35.8%), with a standardized coefficient of −0.43 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). Moreover, plant performance traits (relative importance = 24.6%) were also important for modulating SNF responses to N enrichment, with the standardized coefficient being 0.29 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). The N enrichment rate explained 11.7% of the relative importance in SNF responses with a standardized coefficient of −0.30 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). The remaining variables (i.e., mean annual temperature and microbial traits) collectively accounted for 24.6% of the relative importance in SNF responses (Fig. 3). Moreover, environmental factors indirectly mediated SNF responses upon N enrichment through plant performance trait modification, with a standardized coefficient of −0.56 for mean annual temperature (p < 0.001), 0.11 for N enrichment rate (p < 0.05), 0.41 for soil carbon:N ratio (p < 0.001), and 0.60 for microbial traits (p < 0.001), respectively (Fig. 3b).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Comments on manuscript: NCOMMS-24-62012
The manuscript entitled "Enhanced plant performance counteracts declines in symbiotic nitrogen fixation (SNF) upon
nitrogen enrichment" addressed an important topic of decrease in SNF under N fertilization using a meta-dataset of
published literatures. The main conclusion is that plant performance traits could be a previously neglected drivers of the
SNF responses to N enrichment. Although the finding is interesting, there are quite a lot of flaws to draw this conclusion.
Please see my comments below.
First of all, the knowledge gap of this study is a bit questionable. The study raised a seemly interesting but rarely
demonstrated topic of the SNF responses – SNF remains unexpectedly high in some N-rich ecosystems. Nevertheless,
such knowledge gap, from this study, is mainly based on the observation from ‘free-living’ and ‘associated’ N
fixation, but not ‘symbiotic’ N fixation. For this point, there are quite a few citations that are incorrect or misleading (e.g., Line 59-60).
As a previous N paradox hypothesized, free-living N fixers are active in many tropical forests due to N-homogeneous
distribution (Hedin et al. 2009, also shown in the citation list). This hypothesis has been well demonstrated by many field
studies. By contrast, symbiotic N fixation, performed by legume plants, are quite different. Although there are two N-fixing
strategies (obligate and facultative), both of them face the same fate of disadvantage of SNF under N-rich environment. For
example, facultative N fixers downregulate fixation rates, and obligate N fixers are substituted by non-N fixers. Based on the
fact above, the starting point (knowledge gap) of the study should be re-organized or alternatively, more lines of evidence
are needed for supporting this point.
Additionally, the conceptual framework of plant performance that regulates SNF responses are not persuasive enough.
Particularly, in the Introduction, such possibility is based on relationships of some plant-growth variables, but why ‘Plant
Performance Does Alleviate the Negative N Impacts on SNF’? What is the driver of this observation? Besides, it is difficult to
demonstrate whether N addition/fixation affect plant performance or plant performance affects the responses of SNF. These
issues should be clearly addressed, not only simply basing on certain relationships and observation.
The study aimed to distinguish the contribution from environmental factors and plant performance traits, but the size of the
current dataset is small. Only a few soil properties (e.g., pH, C, and N), microbial biomass and climatic factors were
considered. Many other factors that are also important for supporting SNF process, such as micronutrients (Mo and V),
phosphorus availability, soil moisture, and light availability, were not evaluated. Lack of evaluating these potential factors
could lead to draw a conclusion of ‘low’ contribution from environmental factors.
Importantly, the selected ‘plant performance traits (biomass, N, P, and shoot/root)’ may not be the best predictors. These
variables are usually thought to be affected by N fertilization and SNF. We could expect that N input (from fertilization and
fixation) change plant biomass, N, P, and shoot/root, but it is less thought that these plant-growth variables in turn affect SNF
(or SNF responses). They look like the ‘results’ but not the ‘drivers’. This is particularly true, given that meta-analysis method
is commonly based on relationships of the selective variables, and thus possibly leads to unexpected ‘high’ contribution
observed in this study.
Instead, there are some truly ‘drivers’ like leaf photosynthesis, plant N demand (N pools), and evapotranspiration, which
could change the resource (e.g., carbohydrate) and energy investment of plants into root nodules and SNF. Unfortunately,
such types of variables are not considered in this study.
While different tree species have divergent capacity of SNF, I am happy to see ‘plant species’ being included as an
influencing factor. Furthermore, I would like to see ‘age’ of plants as a predictor, because different ages/growth-phases of N-
fixing plants also show different capacity of SNF. Thus, the age of N-fixing plants may affect SNF in response to N
fertilization and soil N availability.
Minor comments:
L 100. It is unclear why one of the hypotheses is to examine the responses of SNF between cropland and non-cropland
systems? Is there any typical characteristic for cropland systems when you pointed to SNF?
L 103-105. This hypothesis appears to compare by different N fertilization rates, but how it will happen if both types of
systems receive the same rates of N input?
L 106. What does ‘legume populations’ mean? Legume plant biomass, diversity, or root nodule biomass?
L 106-107. This inference is oddness. How to understand the croplands receiving high N fertilization and then additional N
inputs?
L133-134. This result is interesting, but SNF rates, in many previous researches, were usually measured in the labs. MAT
should be a poor predictor compared to soil temperature.
L199. Again, it is NOT clear why make such comparison. Do all the other ecosystems (forests and grasslands) have the
same responses of SNF to N fertilization?
L232. Compare with non-croplands, croplands are affected more by anthropogenic management than environmental factors.
L271-275. As pointed above, N input could change plant biomass, but how to demonstrate that the change in plant biomass
can affect N input (SNF)?
L276. So, photosynthesis is a more effective predictor than biomass.
L292-295. Again, why increase in temperature could offset the declines in SNF? Does it happen in high-latitude areas?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Synopsis
The manuscript by Yao et al. presents a global analysis assessing the importance of plant performance traits (biomass and
shoot:root ratios) when estimating SNF in terrestrial ecosystems and how SNF responds to N enrichment. The authors use a
dataset of 64 papers (908 observations) providing data on SNF rates and various aspects of the ecosystem (abiotic
characteristics as well as plant performance traits). They conclude that while N enrichment decreases SNF under N
enrichment, that including plant performance traits in the model mitigates this SNF decrease (and improves model
predictions of SNF). The authors also note that the declines in SNF are stronger in non-agricultural systems than in
agricultural systems. Overall, the idea of this analysis is a valuable one, but the text focuses so heavily on the statistical
 the statistical
analyses themselves that the biological interpretation for what these results mean in a real-world context is difficult to
discern. Below are a set of general and specific comments that may help the authors improve their work.
General Comments
• A major missing piece to the data/analyses you present is the delineation between different aspects of measuring SNF.
You looked at SNF exclusively in terms of “N fixed per m2 per year” which has N-fixer abundance/biomass “baked in” to the
estimate. I think the crux of the phenomenon you are trying to convey is that even if individual SNF rates (N fixed per unit N-
fixer biomass) decrease with N fertilization, as long as N-fixer biomass increases, this will mitigate those declines. Your
argument as a whole would be much stronger if you could present data on individual SNF rate declines separately from N-
fixer biomass/abundance responses, and then put those together to get the overall response of SNF at the scale of “N fixed
per m2 per year.”
• Is the “plant biomass” performance trait a metric of N-fixer biomass responses, or all plants in the plot? Particularly in non-
agricultural systems, I would assume that some fertilization studies saw an increase in total plant biomass but an exclusion of N-
fixing species under fertilization treatments.
• More information on how you converted data from the papers you used into individual pairs of control-treatment plots is
needed. The discrepancy between the number of individual studies (68) and the number of data points (908) you used is
very large. It’s not uncommon to obtain multiple independent samples from a single study in a meta-analysis, but a >10x
increase in sample size from study to data point seems very large. I also think you should provide justification for using
multiple plots at the same site as independent observations.
• The declines in SNF in response to N enrichment (such as those you report in lines 229-241) are reported in % decline.
What is the unit of N enrichment for these declines? Given that your data points span a range of N enrichment levels, a
single % decline is difficult to understand. In other words, does a 39% decline in SNF mean a 39% decline per X amount of
N added, or simply SNF declines by 39% when N is added regardless of how much N was added?
• It’s difficult to understand what you mean when you say the models with only environmental variables “overpredict the
decline in SNF due to N enrichment relative to the observed decline.” It seems what you’ve done is used the data on SNF
declines and the site-level environmental data to build a statistical model, and then you’ve built a second set of statistical
models that also incorporate plant performance. In the first set (environmental factors only), I can see how only adding in
these factors makes the model a poor predictor (i.e. low R2), but the model shouldn’t systematically over- or under-predict
the observations. The statistical model is made to slightly over-predict some observations and under-predict others in order
to get a “best fit” approximation. I may be missing some fundamental aspect to how you conducted your statistics. If so,
I apologize, but would suggest that this needs to be explained much more clearly.
• The authors make an idle attempt to include an analysis of SNF responses in croplands vs. non-croplands. Not much effort
is made in the introduction to identify the knowledge gap or importance of SNF responses across ecosystem types. At least
one paragraph in the introduction should be dedicated to the importance of SNF responses in differing ecosystem types and
additional text in the discussion focusing on why we might expect these different responses between agricultural and non-
agricultural systems.
Specific Comments
L51-52. This needs to be generalized. Legumes and rhizobia are not the only nodulating plant symbiosis that fixes nitrogen.
Actinorhizal N-fixers and Frankia bacteria also do this and are the dominant N-fixers in many ecosystems. (indeed, it looks
like you include several actinorhizal N-fixers in your analyses (Fig 2a)).
- A follow up point to the delineation between legumes and actinorhizal N-fixers: The prevailing paradigm is that actinorhizal N
fixers have an “obligate fixation strategy” where they fix N at the same rates per unit biomass regardless of ecosystem N
availability. Your data in Fig 2a provide solid evidence that this is not the case (that old paradigm is progressively falling,
which your data add to its demise). This is not particularly relevant to the main ideas of your paper, but an interesting side
use of these data.
L53. There are many more appropriate citations than the Mason paper for the importance of SNF to GPP (SNF really isn’t a
primary focus of that paper). The Davies-Barnard paper (your current citation #4) or Weider et al. 2015 Environmental
Research Letters would be good alternatives.
L55-56. This sentence implies that we have solid evidence for alterations to natural SNF. The Galloway paper certainly does
not discuss that and I’m not sure the rock weathering paper does either. This sentence needs better support, given how
critical it is to the foundation of the paper.
L70. Citation 11 is for a lichen, which is typically considered asymbiotic N fixation (certainly not the legume-rhizobia
symbiosis that the text refers to).
L112-113: Are these two SNF values significantly different from each other or are you describing a general trend?
L115-116: This part of the sentence is a bit unclear
L117: add “is” after SNF?
L145: This may be more accurately described as “approximately one third of the variability”
L150: Rewrite this sentence, the way it reads is a bit unclear
L186: Use another word besides responsibility
L201: Use of the word “minor” seems a bit too strong considering we are talking about global SNF responses (for specific
ecosystem types), the environmental factors accounted for >30% of variation
L209: “indispensable” is very value-based term. “most important” might be a better alternative.
L210: delete or change the word “Besides” in this sentence
Figure 4: Make it more clear which graphs represent croplands and non-croplands by including titles on your graph

L261: Not sure where you get 40.3% from, and are you talking about improvements for overall SNF models or cropland/non-

L273-275. Following up on the general comment on this topic, the plant biomass response to N enrichment could be very
different from the N-fixer biomass response to N enrichment. How did you verify that the response of the entire plant
population is indicative of the biomass responses of N fixers?

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
I perused the entire manuscript entitled “Enhanced plant performance counteracts declines in symbiotic nitrogen fixation
upon nitrogen enrichment” that has been submitted by Yao et al. It is an interesting work and well-presented, and has the
potential for publication. I agree with the authors that plant performance is an indispensable predictor of SNF responses to N
enrichment. However, I still have some comments and hope that these suggestions will be helpful in improving the
manuscript.
(1) My major concern is that the authors try to establish a perspective that plant performance, like the environmental factors
directly regulating the activities of rhizobia, is a potential determinant of SNF responses to N enrichment. Indeed, it has been
widely demonstrated that N enrichment can improve productivity and limit symbiotic nitrogen fixation, thereby impelling the
N-fixing plants to uptake N from the soil relative to that from the SNF. Hence, there might raise a positive association
between the increase in plant performance traits and decrease in SNF. Nevertheless, I do not think the SNF decline directly
results from the increase in plant performance traits. By contrast, the increase in plant performance traits might be due to the
decline of SNF which leads to plants obtaining N from soil by a cheap way rather than the energetically expensive process.
Therefore, I suggest cautiously using some words (counteract, etc.) and providing more detailed information to illustrate how
plant performance traits influence SNF under N enrichment conditions.
(2) Line 53, The “biogeochemical N cycle” should be included in the ecosystem function besides the “gross primary
production”, as the next sentence states the quantity of N introduced into the ecosystem.
(3) Line 55, Not only synthetic N, but also atmospheric deposited N has affected the terrestrial ecosystems and altered the
dynamics of SNF.
(4) Line 66, Please add some references here.
(5) Line 68, I am confused about the phrase “save photosynthates”. Theoretically, the enhanced N input reduces SNF and
the N-fixing plants tend to uptake N by a cheap process with root rather than the high energetic cost process through SNF,
thus leading to the changes in the allocation of photosynthates between above- and below-ground growth.
(6) Line 80, Delete the word “for”.
(7) Line 81, It seems to talk about the same thing with the sentence mentioned above (see line 60-61). Please rephrase
these sentences.
(8) Line 89-90, Many studies have shown that light is a key environmental factor regulating SNF, but the current analysis
does not include light as an environmental factor. Does this reduce the explained proportion of environmental factors to SNF
decline?
(9) Line 90-92, Please add more explanation on how plant performance counteracts the decline of SNF.
(10) Line 106, Why did the authors use “population” instead of “species”, as numerous plant species are examined in this
study?
(11) Line 186-196, It is well known that the N enhancement has a direct effect on soil N availability and subsequently
influence soil C/N. But in the SEM, I am confused about the absence of the relationship between soil C/N and N enrichment.
Besides, please provide the parameters indicating the goodness of the SEM.
(12) Line 271-280, Please provide more explanation on how shoot: root ratio influences SNF, although the authors have
respectively stated the effect of shoot biomass and root traits on SNF. This is important to reveal the mechanisms underlying
the decline of SNF with increasing in shoot: root ratio.
(13) Line 293, The word “reduced” should be “increased”.
(14) Line 314, This word “wild” should be in upright font. In addition, please see comment 11 about “population”.
(15) Line 713, It should be “carbon to nitrogen ratio of soil”.
(16) Line 712, In figure S4, this study found a weak relationship of SNF in response to MAP. I am wondering whether the
authors take irrigation conditions into account for each sampling site in the croplands when analyzing this relationship, as
there should be difference in SNF performance between irrigated and unirrigated plants in the croplands, which might
influence the response of SNF to MAP.

Reviewer #2' comments:
The manuscript by Yao et al. presents a global analysis assessing the importance of
plant performance traits (biomass and shoot:root ratios) when estimating SNF in
terrestrial ecosystems and how SNF responds to N enrichment. The authors use a
dataset of 64 papers (908 observations) providing data on SNF rates and various
aspects of the ecosystem (abiotic characteristics as well as plant performance traits).
They conclude that while N enrichment decreases SNF under N enrichment, that
including plant performance traits in the model mitigates this SNF decrease (and
improves model predictions of SNF). The authors also note that the declines in SNF are
stronger in non-agricultural systems than in agricultural systems. Overall, the idea of
this analysis is a valuable one, but the text focuses so heavily on the statistical
analyses themselves that the biological interpretation for what these results mean in a
real-world context is difficult to discern. Below are a set of general and specific comments that
may help the authors improve their work.
Response: We greatly appreciate the reviewer for the positive and insightful
comments. According to these comments, we have carefully improved the
manuscript.
1. A major missing piece to the data/analyses you present is the delineation between
different aspects of measuring SNF. You looked at SNF exclusively in terms of “N fixed
per m2 per year” which has N-fixer abundance/biomass “baked in” to the estimate. I
think the crux of the phenomenon you are trying to convey is that even if individual SNF
rates (N fixed per unit N-fixer biomass) decrease with N fertilization, as long as N-fixer
biomass increases, this will mitigate those declines. Your argument as a whole would
be much stronger if you could present data on individual SNF rate declines separately
from N-fixer biomass/abundance responses, and then put those together to get the
overall response of SNF at the scale of “N fixed per m2 per year.”
Response: We fully agree with your comment: Total SNF at the ecosystem scale
(e.g., per m² per year) can be decomposed into two components: (1) individual SNF
rate per unit N-fixer biomass and (2) the biomass or abundance of N-fixing plants.
This decomposition would enrich the interpretation of mechanisms behind SNF
responses to N enrichment. In the current study, however, we focused on total SNF
per unit area as the integrated response variable. This decision was made based
on two main considerations:
1. The methods (e.g., 15N isotope techniques and acetylene reduction assay)
used to measure individual SNF rates per unit biomass vary substantially among
primary studies, making meta-analytic synthesis of these values difficult. In
contrast, area-based SNF estimates (e.g., g N m⁻² year⁻¹) are more consistently
reported and allow for higher comparability across sites.
2. The primary goal of this study was to assess whether incorporating plant
performance traits could improve the predictive capacity for SNF responses to
nitrogen enrichment. For this purpose, area-based SNF responses reflect the net
ecological effect - including both physiological and structural changes of N-fixing
plants - and are thus more relevant to large-scale projections and Earth system
model applications.
Despite of these, we appreciate the conceptual importance of decomposing
SNF responses into component processes. We have added a new figure (Figure 5)
in the Supplementary Information that displays the decline of SNF per unit
biomass under N enrichment, based on a subset of studies reporting both total SNF
and biomass. This analysis demonstrates that, on average, N enrichment reduces
the SNF efficiency per unit biomass, supporting the notion that physiological
downregulation plays a role in the observed SNF decline (please see lines 121-123
in revised manuscript).
Lines 121-123: “N enrichment slightly reduced SNF (8.49 g N m-2 year-1 of
SNF upon N enrichment versus 9.51 g N m-2 year-1 upon ambient condition, p =
0.12), partially attributable to decreased SNF per unit biomass (Figure S1).”
We have also added information in the Discussion (please see lines 385-387 in
revised manuscript).
Line 385-387: “Additionally, areal SNF rates (e.g., g N m⁻² year⁻¹) integrate
both physiological efficiency and diazotroph biomass. Though SNF per unit
biomass declined in available subsets (Figure S1), future works are needed to
systematically partition these components.”

all plants in the plot? Particularly in non-agricultural systems, I would assume that
some fertilization studies saw an increase in total plant biomass but an exclusion of N-
fixing species under fertilization treatments.
Response: Thank you very much for your valuable comment. In non-croplands, N
enrichment often suppresses N-fixing plants through increasing competition from
non-N-fixing species. Therefore, it is essential to clarify what is meant by “plant
biomass” in our study.
In this study, plant biomass specifically refers to the biomass of N-fixing
plants, not the total biomass of the plant community. This distinction is crucial to
avoid conflating responses of non-fixing species, which could obscure the
interpretation of SNF responses. Studies that only provided community-level
biomass, or failed to isolate N-fixing plant responses, were excluded from our
synthesis.
To avoid ambiguity, we have revised the manuscript by (1) consistently
referring to “N-fixing plant biomass” throughout the text, and (2) explicitly stating
this definition (please see lines 427-430 in revised manuscript).

ratios, plant N and phosphorus contents) refer exclusively to N-fixing species
rather than community-level vegetation, ensuring SNF responses reflect

in a meta-analysis, but a >10x increase in sample size from study to data point seems
very large. I also think you should provide justification for using multiple plots at the
same site as independent observations.
Response: Thanks for this valuable comment. To clarify, each unique comparison
between a nitrogen-enriched treatment and its corresponding control - regarding
plant species, N levels, or experimental units - was treated as an independent
observation. Importantly, we retained multiple observations from the same study
only when they were clearly independent in experimental design - for example, if
they represented different species, different treatment intensities, or spatially
separated plots. The substantial variation in SNF responses among different N-
fixing species, even under similar environmental conditions, supports this
approach (please see lines 419-421 in revised manuscript).
Line 419-421: “where each unique comparison between a treatment and its
corresponding control - defined by distinct species, N levels, or experimental units
- constituted an independent observation.”
Furthermore, to more rigorously address statistical dependencies introduced
by shared control groups, we incorporated a variance–covariance matrix into the
meta-analysis. This matrix explicitly captures the non-independence among lnRR
values derived from multiple treatment groups sharing the same control group
within a study (please see lines 455-481 in revised manuscript).
Moreover, we also used linear mixed-effect models with study ID as random
effects to account for the variation among studies (please see lines 490-495 in
revised manuscript).

Reviewer #2' comments:
The manuscript by Yao et al. presents a global analysis assessing the importance of
plant performance traits (biomass and shoot:root ratios) when estimating SNF in
terrestrial ecosystems and how SNF responds to N enrichment. The authors have done a thorough job of addressing the comments from the initial set

the direction of causality between plant trait responses and SNF responses to N
enrichment. The description of how the authors got 908 observations from 68 studies
also improved substantially.
Response: We greatly appreciate the reviewer’s positive comments.
1. However, with the clarity provided in the updated description, I am less convinced of
the fundamental value of the analysis. In the end, the main conclusion of the paper is
“N additions decrease SNF, but N additions also make N fixers grow larger, which
dampens the negative effect of N additions on SNF.” This is an interesting finding, but
without the ability to link any mechanistic causality to the analyses, it is hard to envision
how this conclusion would be used in future endeavors such as Earth System Models.
Model development typically relies on improved mechanistic understanding of the
regulation of SNF rather than phenomenological correlations.
Response: Thank the reviewer for this insightful advice. We agree that a
mechanistic understanding, rather than a purely phenomenological correlation, is
critical for the developing of Earth System Models. However, effectively
incorporating the mechanistic understanding into Earth System Models is a
fundamental challenge, as environmental heterogeneity complicates the direct
extrapolation to macroscales. Scaling up is a crucial step in reconciling microscale
mechanistic insights with macroscale predictive frameworks (Li et al., 2025,
accepted by Frontiers of Earth Science). Global analyses, such as those presented
in our study, allow scaling up the mechanistic understanding of the compensatory
SNF supported by plant growth under N enrichment by accounting for both direct
and indirect effects in Earth System Models. In the revised manuscript, we have
expanded the Discussion to explicitly bridge our findings with model parameters
and their applicability for model predictions (please see lines 318-319, 321-323,
and 385-388 in the revised manuscript).
Moreover, our work enables the quantitative partitioning of the positive effect
of N-fixer growth from the negative effect of N deposition on biological N fixation,
although a complete reformulation of Earth System Models remains aspirational.
Importantly, the relative contribution of these two components varies significantly
across ecosystems—legumes in croplands exhibit stronger compensatory gains
than those in non-croplands (Table 1), highlighting the need for ecosystem-specific
parameterizations in model development. In our revised manuscript, we have
elaborated on how these identified mechanisms can be incorporated and
parameterized (Eqns 8 and 9) within Earth System Model frameworks (please see
lines 364-368, 388-392, 392-396, and 396-398 in the revised manuscript).

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Anthropogenic nitrogen enrichment is widely expected to suppress symbiotic nitrogen fixation in terrestrial ecosystems. Nevertheless, observed symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses remain incompletely explained by exogenous nitrogen inputs, climate, and edaphic factors. In this meta-analysis, we integrate 908 globally distributed field measurements to identify the key predictors that improve simulation of symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses to nitrogen enrichment. On average, symbiotic nitrogen fixation declines by 33.0% upon nitrogen enrichment, with the reduction being more pronounced in non-croplands than croplands. Models considering only environmental factors overestimate symbiotic nitrogen fixation decline relative to observations. The better performance of plant traits like plant growth and biomass allocation (shoot:root ratio) partially buffers symbiotic nitrogen fixation suppression under nitrogen enrichment. Integrating both environmental factors and plant performance traits improves predictive accuracy of symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses by 42.7% and brings the simulated symbiotic nitrogen fixation reductions into close agreement with observations. The alterations in plant performance traits are thus critical for explaining variability in terrestrial symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses, and incorporating plant trait dynamics in Earth System Models can quantitatively partition the compensatory symbiotic nitrogen fixation supported by nitrogen-fixing plant growth from the direct negative impact of nitrogen inputs.

---

## Introduction

Symbiotic nitrogen (N) fixation (SNF), carried out by plant-microbe symbionts (e.g., rhizobia and Frankia), sustains critical terrestrial ecosystem functions, including biogeochemical N cycling and gross primary production1,2. Globally, SNF replenishes 50-70 Tg N yr−1 in croplands3,4 and 31-66 Tg N yr−1 in non-croplands1,4. Anthropogenic N enrichment, especially via atmospheric deposition and synthetic fertilizer inputs, has markedly altered SNF dynamics5,6. Consistent with carbon-economic theory, the declines in SNF under exogenous N sufficiency are confirmed, particularly for facultative fixers7,8. Yet the observed magnitude of N-induced SNF suppression remains poorly predicted by environmental factors alone9. In particular, substantial taxon-specific variation persists under comparable conditions10–12, implicating unaccounted plant traits (e.g., performance traits) as key regulators. However, the role of plant performance traits in predicting SNF responses to N enrichment remains largely overlooked, particularly at large spatial scales.

A comprehensive understanding of SNF responses and their predictors is essential to project terrestrial N budgets accurately, thus informing ecosystem functionality assessments under anthropogenic change.

Environmental factors, including exogenous N inputs, climate, and edaphic conditions, have been extensively investigated for their roles in regulationg SNF responses9,13. Carbon-economic theory posits that exogenous N inputs (e.g., nitrate and ammonium enrichment) suppress legume SNF, as direct N uptake is energetically cheaper than maintaining N-fixing symbionts14,15. Accordingly, legumes in N-rich conditions preferentially assimilate soil bioavailable N while down-regulating SNF16,17, thereby weakening plant-microbe mutualism under N enrichment18. This suppression operates mechanistically through reduced rhizobia colonization, diminished rhizobia populations, and curtailed nodule biomass17,19,20. Climatic and edaphic factors can also modulate SNF sensitivity to N enrichment. For instance, SNF declines upon N enrichment were less pronounced at high mean annual temperatures9, while elevated soil carbon: N ratios and pH buffer diazotrophs against N inhibition13 and consequently attenuate SNF declines. Despite the importance of environmental factors, these factors explain only 2-33% of observed variation in SNF responses upon N enrichment9,13, leaving a large proportion of variability attributable to unidentified predictors.

Plant performance traits emerge as critical predictors of SNF responses to environmental change. Biomass allocation patterns substantially contribute to observed SNF variability21, e.g., in Glycine max, SNF increases by 35% as shoot biomass rises from 842.9 g m−2 to 1200.2 g m−2 22, while root biomass consistently correlates with SNF magnitude21. Higher shoot:root ratios often correlate with enhanced SNF, potentially through improved light interception, as light availability is a key factor regulating the symbiotic efficiency of legumes23,24. Given that N enrichment frequently enhances biomass accumulation and shoot:root ratios in N-fixing plants25–27, these trait adjustments may partially alleviate SNF declines by augmenting photosynthetic capacity and carbon supply to fuel energetically costly N fixation. Accordingly, we hypothesized that plant trait plasticity may explain a significant fraction of the residual heterogeneity in SNF responses to N enrichment (Hypothesis 1). Critically, the quantitative global-scale contribution of plant performance traits to SNF responses, beyond environmental predictors, has yet to be assessed.

Divergent baseline N conditions between non-croplands and croplands due to long-term anthropogenic management can fundamentally alter SNF responses to experimental N enrichment. Chronic fertilization in croplands elevates soil N availability while simultaneously disrupting legume-rhizobia mutualism and reshaping microbial communities28,29. Consequently, legumes in croplands may acclimatize to high exogenous N inputs and exhibit attenuated SNF sensitivity relative to non-croplands18,30,31. In contrast, N-fixing plants in non-croplands experience more marked declines in nodule biomass and SNF following N inputs due to limited microbial adaptation, abrupt symbiosis breakdown, and competitive exclusion pressure from non-fixing species7,32,33. Accordingly, we propose that N enrichment suppresses SNF more markedly in non-croplands than croplands (Hypothesis 2).

This study focuses on accurate SNF predictability rather than mechanistic causation, to identify plant predictors explaining heterogeneity in SNF responses to N enrichment across sites and taxa. Leveraging a global synthesis based on 908 field observations, we determine the dominant predictors of SNF responses to N enrichment. Two specific questions were addressed: (a) What proportion of variability in SNF responses is explained by environmental factors (exogenous N inputs, climate, and edaphic properties) versus plant performance traits? (b) What are the differences in SNF responses between croplands and non-croplands?

---

## Results

Environmental forces are insufficient to explain SNF responses upon N enrichment

N enrichment reduced SNF (8.49 g N m−2 yr−1 of SNF upon N enrichment versus 9.51 g N m−2 yr−1 upon ambient conditions), partially attributable to decreased SNF per unit biomass (Fig. S1). On average, the weighted effect size of SNF was −0.40 (95% CI: –0.58 ~ −0.22), corresponding to a 33.0% global decline relative to controls (Fig. 1a). This suppression in SNF intensified poleward (slope = −0.01, p < 0.05) (Fig. S2), and SNF decline was aggravated with high levels of N enrichment rate (a slope of −0.16, p < 0.01) (Fig. 1b).

Environmental factors partially accounted for the global variation in SNF responses to N enrichment (Fig. S3). SNF decline attenuated in conditions with higher mean annual temperature (slope = 0.42, p < 0.05), while the effects of precipitation on SNF response were insignificant (p = 0.50; Fig. S3a, b). Edaphically, SNF decline amplified under lower soil pH (slope = 0.21, p < 0.05), greater carbon:N ratio (slope = −0.53, p < 0.05), and elevated available phosphorus (slope = −0.32, p < 0.05). Ambient soil ammonium (p = 0.17) and nitrate (p = 0.66) exerted negligible influences (Fig. S3c–g). Moreover, SNF decline was more pronounced in soils with higher microbial biomass carbon (slope = −0.33, p < 0.05) and microbial biomass N (slope = −0.41, p < 0.05) (Fig. S3h–i). Notably, N enrichment rate (relative importance = 37.4%) and soil carbon:N ratio (relative importance = 31.4%) emerged as dominant predictors of the variability of SNF responses at a global scale (Fig. 1). The combined factors (i.e., mean annual temperature, N enrichment rate, pH, soil carbon:N ratio, available phosphorus, the carbon and N contents in microbial biomass) explained approximately one third of the variability of SNF responses at a global scale (34.2%) (Fig. 1c).

Enhancement of plant performance traits ameliorated the SNF decline upon N enrichment

SNF response to N enrichment also diverged across plant taxa (ranging from −1.29 to 0.44; Fig. 2a). Plant trait plasticity buffers SNF declines upon N enrichment. The enhanced N-fixing plant biomass or shoot:root ratios upon N enrichment attenuated SNF decline, while changes in plant nutrient contents had little impact on SNF responses (Fig. 2). Specifically, SNF decline trended to neutralize with the enhancement of plant performance traits, with a slope of 0.47 for N-fixing plant biomass (p < 0.001) and 2.75 for the plant shoot:root ratios (p < 0.01), respectively (Fig. 2).

Integrating plant performance traits, soil properties, microbial traits, N enrichment rate, and climatic factors explained 48.8% of the variability in SNF responses to N enrichment (Fig. 3). This represents a substantial improvement of 42.7% (a relative increase in explanatory power) over the prediction considering merely environmental factors (34.2% explained variance in Fig. 1c), which was consistently confirmed by both linear mixed-effects model and structural equation model (SEM). In the SEM, soil carbon:N ratio was the crucial driver of the variability in SNF responses to N enrichment (relative importance = 35.8%), with a standardized coefficient of −0.43 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). Moreover, plant performance traits (relative importance = 24.6%) were also important for modulating SNF responses to N enrichment, with the standardized coefficient being 0.29 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). The N enrichment rate explained 11.7% of the relative importance in SNF responses with a standardized coefficient of −0.30 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). The remaining variables (i.e., mean annual temperature and microbial traits) collectively accounted for 24.6% of the relative importance in SNF responses (Fig. 3). Moreover, environmental factors indirectly mediated SNF responses upon N enrichment through plant performance trait modification, with a standardized coefficient of −0.56 for mean annual temperature (p < 0.001), 0.11 for N enrichment rate (p < 0.05), 0.41 for soil carbon:N ratio (p < 0.001), and 0.60 for microbial traits (p < 0.001), respectively (Fig. 3b).

## Paper

## Abstract

Anthropogenic nitrogen enrichment is widely expected to suppress symbiotic nitrogen fixation in terrestrial ecosystems. Nevertheless, observed symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses remain incompletely explained by exogenous nitrogen inputs, climate, and edaphic factors. In this meta-analysis, we integrate 908 globally distributed field measurements to identify the key predictors that improve simulation of symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses to nitrogen enrichment. On average, symbiotic nitrogen fixation declines by 33.0% upon nitrogen enrichment, with the reduction being more pronounced in non-croplands than croplands. Models considering only environmental factors overestimate symbiotic nitrogen fixation decline relative to observations. The better performance of plant traits like plant growth and biomass allocation (shoot:root ratio) partially buffers symbiotic nitrogen fixation suppression under nitrogen enrichment. Integrating both environmental factors and plant performance traits improves predictive accuracy of symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses by 42.7% and brings the simulated symbiotic nitrogen fixation reductions into close agreement with observations. The alterations in plant performance traits are thus critical for explaining variability in terrestrial symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses, and incorporating plant trait dynamics in Earth System Models can quantitatively partition the compensatory symbiotic nitrogen fixation supported by nitrogen-fixing plant growth from the direct negative impact of nitrogen inputs.

---

## Introduction

Symbiotic nitrogen (N) fixation (SNF), carried out by plant-microbe symbionts (e.g., rhizobia and Frankia), sustains critical terrestrial ecosystem functions, including biogeochemical N cycling and gross primary production1,2. Globally, SNF replenishes 50-70 Tg N yr−1 in croplands3,4 and 31-66 Tg N yr−1 in non-croplands1,4. Anthropogenic N enrichment, especially via atmospheric deposition and synthetic fertilizer inputs, has markedly altered SNF dynamics5,6. Consistent with carbon-economic theory, the declines in SNF under exogenous N sufficiency are confirmed, particularly for facultative fixers7,8. Yet the observed magnitude of N-induced SNF suppression remains poorly predicted by environmental factors alone9. In particular, substantial taxon-specific variation persists under comparable conditions10–12, implicating unaccounted plant traits (e.g., performance traits) as key regulators. However, the role of plant performance traits in predicting SNF responses to N enrichment remains largely overlooked, particularly at large spatial scales.

A comprehensive understanding of SNF responses and their predictors is essential to project terrestrial N budgets accurately, thus informing ecosystem functionality assessments under anthropogenic change.

Environmental factors, including exogenous N inputs, climate, and edaphic conditions, have been extensively investigated for their roles in regulationg SNF responses9,13. Carbon-economic theory posits that exogenous N inputs (e.g., nitrate and ammonium enrichment) suppress legume SNF, as direct N uptake is energetically cheaper than maintaining N-fixing symbionts14,15. Accordingly, legumes in N-rich conditions preferentially assimilate soil bioavailable N while down-regulating SNF16,17, thereby weakening plant-microbe mutualism under N enrichment18. This suppression operates mechanistically through reduced rhizobia colonization, diminished rhizobia populations, and curtailed nodule biomass17,19,20. Climatic and edaphic factors can also modulate SNF sensitivity to N enrichment. For instance, SNF declines upon N enrichment were less pronounced at high mean annual temperatures9, while elevated soil carbon: N ratios and pH buffer diazotrophs against N inhibition13 and consequently attenuate SNF declines. Despite the importance of environmental factors, these factors explain only 2-33% of observed variation in SNF responses upon N enrichment9,13, leaving a large proportion of variability attributable to unidentified predictors.

Plant performance traits emerge as critical predictors of SNF responses to environmental change. Biomass allocation patterns substantially contribute to observed SNF variability21, e.g., in Glycine max, SNF increases by 35% as shoot biomass rises from 842.9 g m−2 to 1200.2 g m−2 22, while root biomass consistently correlates with SNF magnitude21. Higher shoot:root ratios often correlate with enhanced SNF, potentially through improved light interception, as light availability is a key factor regulating the symbiotic efficiency of legumes23,24. Given that N enrichment frequently enhances biomass accumulation and shoot:root ratios in N-fixing plants25–27, these trait adjustments may partially alleviate SNF declines by augmenting photosynthetic capacity and carbon supply to fuel energetically costly N fixation. Accordingly, we hypothesized that plant trait plasticity may explain a significant fraction of the residual heterogeneity in SNF responses to N enrichment (Hypothesis 1). Critically, the quantitative global-scale contribution of plant performance traits to SNF responses, beyond environmental predictors, has yet to be assessed.

Divergent baseline N conditions between non-croplands and croplands due to long-term anthropogenic management can fundamentally alter SNF responses to experimental N enrichment. Chronic fertilization in croplands elevates soil N availability while simultaneously disrupting legume-rhizobia mutualism and reshaping microbial communities28,29. Consequently, legumes in croplands may acclimatize to high exogenous N inputs and exhibit attenuated SNF sensitivity relative to non-croplands18,30,31. In contrast, N-fixing plants in non-croplands experience more marked declines in nodule biomass and SNF following N inputs due to limited microbial adaptation, abrupt symbiosis breakdown, and competitive exclusion pressure from non-fixing species7,32,33. Accordingly, we propose that N enrichment suppresses SNF more markedly in non-croplands than croplands (Hypothesis 2).

This study focuses on accurate SNF predictability rather than mechanistic causation, to identify plant predictors explaining heterogeneity in SNF responses to N enrichment across sites and taxa. Leveraging a global synthesis based on 908 field observations, we determine the dominant predictors of SNF responses to N enrichment. Two specific questions were addressed: (a) What proportion of variability in SNF responses is explained by environmental factors (exogenous N inputs, climate, and edaphic properties) versus plant performance traits? (b) What are the differences in SNF responses between croplands and non-croplands?

---

## Results

Environmental forces are insufficient to explain SNF responses upon N enrichment

N enrichment reduced SNF (8.49 g N m−2 yr−1 of SNF upon N enrichment versus 9.51 g N m−2 yr−1 upon ambient conditions), partially attributable to decreased SNF per unit biomass (Fig. S1). On average, the weighted effect size of SNF was −0.40 (95% CI: –0.58 ~ −0.22), corresponding to a 33.0% global decline relative to controls (Fig. 1a). This suppression in SNF intensified poleward (slope = −0.01, p < 0.05) (Fig. S2), and SNF decline was aggravated with high levels of N enrichment rate (a slope of −0.16, p < 0.01) (Fig. 1b).

Environmental factors partially accounted for the global variation in SNF responses to N enrichment (Fig. S3). SNF decline attenuated in conditions with higher mean annual temperature (slope = 0.42, p < 0.05), while the effects of precipitation on SNF response were insignificant (p = 0.50; Fig. S3a, b). Edaphically, SNF decline amplified under lower soil pH (slope = 0.21, p < 0.05), greater carbon:N ratio (slope = −0.53, p < 0.05), and elevated available phosphorus (slope = −0.32, p < 0.05). Ambient soil ammonium (p = 0.17) and nitrate (p = 0.66) exerted negligible influences (Fig. S3c–g). Moreover, SNF decline was more pronounced in soils with higher microbial biomass carbon (slope = −0.33, p < 0.05) and microbial biomass N (slope = −0.41, p < 0.05) (Fig. S3h–i). Notably, N enrichment rate (relative importance = 37.4%) and soil carbon:N ratio (relative importance = 31.4%) emerged as dominant predictors of the variability of SNF responses at a global scale (Fig. 1). The combined factors (i.e., mean annual temperature, N enrichment rate, pH, soil carbon:N ratio, available phosphorus, the carbon and N contents in microbial biomass) explained approximately one third of the variability of SNF responses at a global scale (34.2%) (Fig. 1c).

Enhancement of plant performance traits ameliorated the SNF decline upon N enrichment

SNF response to N enrichment also diverged across plant taxa (ranging from −1.29 to 0.44; Fig. 2a). Plant trait plasticity buffers SNF declines upon N enrichment. The enhanced N-fixing plant biomass or shoot:root ratios upon N enrichment attenuated SNF decline, while changes in plant nutrient contents had little impact on SNF responses (Fig. 2). Specifically, SNF decline trended to neutralize with the enhancement of plant performance traits, with a slope of 0.47 for N-fixing plant biomass (p < 0.001) and 2.75 for the plant shoot:root ratios (p < 0.01), respectively (Fig. 2).

Integrating plant performance traits, soil properties, microbial traits, N enrichment rate, and climatic factors explained 48.8% of the variability in SNF responses to N enrichment (Fig. 3). This represents a substantial improvement of 42.7% (a relative increase in explanatory power) over the prediction considering merely environmental factors (34.2% explained variance in Fig. 1c), which was consistently confirmed by both linear mixed-effects model and structural equation model (SEM). In the SEM, soil carbon:N ratio was the crucial driver of the variability in SNF responses to N enrichment (relative importance = 35.8%), with a standardized coefficient of −0.43 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). Moreover, plant performance traits (relative importance = 24.6%) were also important for modulating SNF responses to N enrichment, with the standardized coefficient being 0.29 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). The N enrichment rate explained 11.7% of the relative importance in SNF responses with a standardized coefficient of −0.30 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). The remaining variables (i.e., mean annual temperature and microbial traits) collectively accounted for 24.6% of the relative importance in SNF responses (Fig. 3). Moreover, environmental factors indirectly mediated SNF responses upon N enrichment through plant performance trait modification, with a standardized coefficient of −0.56 for mean annual temperature (p < 0.001), 0.11 for N enrichment rate (p < 0.05), 0.41 for soil carbon:N ratio (p < 0.001), and 0.60 for microbial traits (p < 0.001), respectively (Fig. 3b).

Synopsis
The manuscript by Yao et al. presents a global analysis assessing the importance of plant performance traits (biomass and
shoot:root ratios) when estimating SNF in terrestrial ecosystems and how SNF responds to N enrichment. The authors use a
dataset of 64 papers (908 observations) providing data on SNF rates and various aspects of the ecosystem (abiotic
characteristics as well as plant performance traits). They conclude that while N enrichment decreases SNF under N
enrichment, that including plant performance traits in the model mitigates this SNF decrease (and improves model
predictions of SNF). The authors also note that the declines in SNF are stronger in non-agricultural systems than in
agricultural systems. Overall, the idea of this analysis is a valuable one, but the text focuses so heavily on the statistical
 the statistical
analyses themselves that the biological interpretation for what these results mean in a real-world context is difficult to
discern. Below are a set of general and specific comments that may help the authors improve their work.
General Comments
• A major missing piece to the data/analyses you present is the delineation between different aspects of measuring SNF.
You looked at SNF exclusively in terms of “N fixed per m2 per year” which has N-fixer abundance/biomass “baked in” to the
estimate. I think the crux of the phenomenon you are trying to convey is that even if individual SNF rates (N fixed per unit N-
fixer biomass) decrease with N fertilization, as long as N-fixer biomass increases, this will mitigate those declines. Your
argument as a whole would be much stronger if you could present data on individual SNF rate declines separately from N-
fixer biomass/abundance responses, and then put those together to get the overall response of SNF at the scale of “N fixed
per m2 per year.”
• Is the “plant biomass” performance trait a metric of N-fixer biomass responses, or all plants in the plot? Particularly in non-
agricultural systems, I would assume that some fertilization studies saw an increase in total plant biomass but an exclusion of N-
fixing species under fertilization treatments.
• More information on how you converted data from the papers you used into individual pairs of control-treatment plots is
needed. The discrepancy between the number of individual studies (68) and the number of data points (908) you used is
very large. It’s not uncommon to obtain multiple independent samples from a single study in a meta-analysis, but a >10x
increase in sample size from study to data point seems very large. I also think you should provide justification for using
multiple plots at the same site as independent observations.

single % decline is difficult to understand. In other words, does a 39% decline in SNF mean a 39% decline per X amount of
N added, or simply SNF declines by 39% when N is added regardless of how much N was added?

decline in SNF due to N enrichment relative to the observed decline.” It seems what you’ve done is used the data on SNF

plant performance traits (biomass and shoot:root ratios) when estimating SNF in
terrestrial ecosystems and how SNF responds to N enrichment. The authors use a
dataset of 64 papers (908 observations) providing data on SNF rates and various
aspects of the ecosystem (abiotic characteristics as well as plant performance traits).
They conclude that while N enrichment decreases SNF under N enrichment, that
including plant performance traits in the model mitigates this SNF decrease (and
improves model predictions of SNF). The authors also note that the declines in SNF are
stronger in non-agricultural systems than in agricultural systems. Overall, the idea of
this analysis is a valuable one, but the text focuses so heavily on the statistical
analyses themselves that the biological interpretation for what these results mean in a
real-world context is difficult to discern. Below are a set of general and specific comments that
may help the authors improve their work.

1. A major missing piece to the data/analyses you present is the delineation between
different aspects of measuring SNF. You looked at SNF exclusively in terms of “N fixed
per m2 per year” which has N-fixer abundance/biomass “baked in” to the estimate. I
think the crux of the phenomenon you are trying to convey is that even if individual SNF
rates (N fixed per unit N-fixer biomass) decrease with N fertilization, as long as N-fixer
biomass increases, this will mitigate those declines. Your argument as a whole would
be much stronger if you could present data on individual SNF rate declines separately
from N-fixer biomass/abundance responses, and then put those together to get the
overall response of SNF at the scale of “N fixed per m2 per year.”
Response: We fully agree with your comment: Total SNF at the ecosystem scale
(e.g., per m² per year) can be decomposed into two components: (1) individual SNF
rate per unit N-fixer biomass and (2) the biomass or abundance of N-fixing plants.
This decomposition would enrich the interpretation of mechanisms behind SNF
responses to N enrichment. In the current study, however, we focused on total SNF
per unit area as the integrated response variable. This decision was made based
on two main considerations:
1. The methods (e.g., 15N isotope techniques and acetylene reduction assay)
used to measure individual SNF rates per unit biomass vary substantially among
primary studies, making meta-analytic synthesis of these values difficult. In
contrast, area-based SNF estimates (e.g., g N m⁻² year⁻¹) are more consistently
reported and allow for higher comparability across sites.

performance traits could improve the predictive capacity for SNF responses to
nitrogen enrichment. For this purpose, area-based SNF responses reflect the net
ecological effect - including both physiological and structural changes of N-fixing
plants - and are thus more relevant to large-scale projections and Earth system
model applications.

## Paper

## Abstract

Anthropogenic nitrogen enrichment is widely expected to suppress symbiotic nitrogen fixation in terrestrial ecosystems. Nevertheless, observed symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses remain incompletely explained by exogenous nitrogen inputs, climate, and edaphic factors. In this meta-analysis, we integrate 908 globally distributed field measurements to identify the key predictors that improve simulation of symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses to nitrogen enrichment. On average, symbiotic nitrogen fixation declines by 33.0% upon nitrogen enrichment, with the reduction being more pronounced in non-croplands than croplands. Models considering only environmental factors overestimate symbiotic nitrogen fixation decline relative to observations. The better performance of plant traits like plant growth and biomass allocation (shoot:root ratio) partially buffers symbiotic nitrogen fixation suppression under nitrogen enrichment. Integrating both environmental factors and plant performance traits improves predictive accuracy of symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses by 42.7% and brings the simulated symbiotic nitrogen fixation reductions into close agreement with observations. The alterations in plant performance traits are thus critical for explaining variability in terrestrial symbiotic nitrogen fixation responses, and incorporating plant trait dynamics in Earth System Models can quantitatively partition the compensatory symbiotic nitrogen fixation supported by nitrogen-fixing plant growth from the direct negative impact of nitrogen inputs.

---

## Introduction

Symbiotic nitrogen (N) fixation (SNF), carried out by plant-microbe symbionts (e.g., rhizobia and Frankia), sustains critical terrestrial ecosystem functions, including biogeochemical N cycling and gross primary production1,2. Globally, SNF replenishes 50-70 Tg N yr−1 in croplands3,4 and 31-66 Tg N yr−1 in non-croplands1,4. Anthropogenic N enrichment, especially via atmospheric deposition and synthetic fertilizer inputs, has markedly altered SNF dynamics5,6. Consistent with carbon-economic theory, the declines in SNF under exogenous N sufficiency are confirmed, particularly for facultative fixers7,8. Yet the observed magnitude of N-induced SNF suppression remains poorly predicted by environmental factors alone9. In particular, substantial taxon-specific variation persists under comparable conditions10–12, implicating unaccounted plant traits (e.g., performance traits) as key regulators. However, the role of plant performance traits in predicting SNF responses to N enrichment remains largely overlooked, particularly at large spatial scales.

A comprehensive understanding of SNF responses and their predictors is essential to project terrestrial N budgets accurately, thus informing ecosystem functionality assessments under anthropogenic change.

Environmental factors, including exogenous N inputs, climate, and edaphic conditions, have been extensively investigated for their roles in regulationg SNF responses9,13. Carbon-economic theory posits that exogenous N inputs (e.g., nitrate and ammonium enrichment) suppress legume SNF, as direct N uptake is energetically cheaper than maintaining N-fixing symbionts14,15. Accordingly, legumes in N-rich conditions preferentially assimilate soil bioavailable N while down-regulating SNF16,17, thereby weakening plant-microbe mutualism under N enrichment18. This suppression operates mechanistically through reduced rhizobia colonization, diminished rhizobia populations, and curtailed nodule biomass17,19,20. Climatic and edaphic factors can also modulate SNF sensitivity to N enrichment. For instance, SNF declines upon N enrichment were less pronounced at high mean annual temperatures9, while elevated soil carbon: N ratios and pH buffer diazotrophs against N inhibition13 and consequently attenuate SNF declines. Despite the importance of environmental factors, these factors explain only 2-33% of observed variation in SNF responses upon N enrichment9,13, leaving a large proportion of variability attributable to unidentified predictors.

Plant performance traits emerge as critical predictors of SNF responses to environmental change. Biomass allocation patterns substantially contribute to observed SNF variability21, e.g., in Glycine max, SNF increases by 35% as shoot biomass rises from 842.9 g m−2 to 1200.2 g m−2 22, while root biomass consistently correlates with SNF magnitude21. Higher shoot:root ratios often correlate with enhanced SNF, potentially through improved light interception, as light availability is a key factor regulating the symbiotic efficiency of legumes23,24. Given that N enrichment frequently enhances biomass accumulation and shoot:root ratios in N-fixing plants25–27, these trait adjustments may partially alleviate SNF declines by augmenting photosynthetic capacity and carbon supply to fuel energetically costly N fixation. Accordingly, we hypothesized that plant trait plasticity may explain a significant fraction of the residual heterogeneity in SNF responses to N enrichment (Hypothesis 1). Critically, the quantitative global-scale contribution of plant performance traits to SNF responses, beyond environmental predictors, has yet to be assessed.

Divergent baseline N conditions between non-croplands and croplands due to long-term anthropogenic management can fundamentally alter SNF responses to experimental N enrichment. Chronic fertilization in croplands elevates soil N availability while simultaneously disrupting legume-rhizobia mutualism and reshaping microbial communities28,29. Consequently, legumes in croplands may acclimatize to high exogenous N inputs and exhibit attenuated SNF sensitivity relative to non-croplands18,30,31. In contrast, N-fixing plants in non-croplands experience more marked declines in nodule biomass and SNF following N inputs due to limited microbial adaptation, abrupt symbiosis breakdown, and competitive exclusion pressure from non-fixing species7,32,33. Accordingly, we propose that N enrichment suppresses SNF more markedly in non-croplands than croplands (Hypothesis 2).

This study focuses on accurate SNF predictability rather than mechanistic causation, to identify plant predictors explaining heterogeneity in SNF responses to N enrichment across sites and taxa. Leveraging a global synthesis based on 908 field observations, we determine the dominant predictors of SNF responses to N enrichment. Two specific questions were addressed: (a) What proportion of variability in SNF responses is explained by environmental factors (exogenous N inputs, climate, and edaphic properties) versus plant performance traits? (b) What are the differences in SNF responses between croplands and non-croplands?

---

## Results

Environmental forces are insufficient to explain SNF responses upon N enrichment

N enrichment reduced SNF (8.49 g N m−2 yr−1 of SNF upon N enrichment versus 9.51 g N m−2 yr−1 upon ambient conditions), partially attributable to decreased SNF per unit biomass (Fig. S1). On average, the weighted effect size of SNF was −0.40 (95% CI: –0.58 ~ −0.22), corresponding to a 33.0% global decline relative to controls (Fig. 1a). This suppression in SNF intensified poleward (slope = −0.01, p < 0.05) (Fig. S2), and SNF decline was aggravated with high levels of N enrichment rate (a slope of −0.16, p < 0.01) (Fig. 1b).

Environmental factors partially accounted for the global variation in SNF responses to N enrichment (Fig. S3). SNF decline attenuated in conditions with higher mean annual temperature (slope = 0.42, p < 0.05), while the effects of precipitation on SNF response were insignificant (p = 0.50; Fig. S3a, b). Edaphically, SNF decline amplified under lower soil pH (slope = 0.21, p < 0.05), greater carbon:N ratio (slope = −0.53, p < 0.05), and elevated available phosphorus (slope = −0.32, p < 0.05). Ambient soil ammonium (p = 0.17) and nitrate (p = 0.66) exerted negligible influences (Fig. S3c–g). Moreover, SNF decline was more pronounced in soils with higher microbial biomass carbon (slope = −0.33, p < 0.05) and microbial biomass N (slope = −0.41, p < 0.05) (Fig. S3h–i). Notably, N enrichment rate (relative importance = 37.4%) and soil carbon:N ratio (relative importance = 31.4%) emerged as dominant predictors of the variability of SNF responses at a global scale (Fig. 1). The combined factors (i.e., mean annual temperature, N enrichment rate, pH, soil carbon:N ratio, available phosphorus, the carbon and N contents in microbial biomass) explained approximately one third of the variability of SNF responses at a global scale (34.2%) (Fig. 1c).

Enhancement of plant performance traits ameliorated the SNF decline upon N enrichment

SNF response to N enrichment also diverged across plant taxa (ranging from −1.29 to 0.44; Fig. 2a). Plant trait plasticity buffers SNF declines upon N enrichment. The enhanced N-fixing plant biomass or shoot:root ratios upon N enrichment attenuated SNF decline, while changes in plant nutrient contents had little impact on SNF responses (Fig. 2). Specifically, SNF decline trended to neutralize with the enhancement of plant performance traits, with a slope of 0.47 for N-fixing plant biomass (p < 0.001) and 2.75 for the plant shoot:root ratios (p < 0.01), respectively (Fig. 2).

Integrating plant performance traits, soil properties, microbial traits, N enrichment rate, and climatic factors explained 48.8% of the variability in SNF responses to N enrichment (Fig. 3). This represents a substantial improvement of 42.7% (a relative increase in explanatory power) over the prediction considering merely environmental factors (34.2% explained variance in Fig. 1c), which was consistently confirmed by both linear mixed-effects model and structural equation model (SEM). In the SEM, soil carbon:N ratio was the crucial driver of the variability in SNF responses to N enrichment (relative importance = 35.8%), with a standardized coefficient of −0.43 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). Moreover, plant performance traits (relative importance = 24.6%) were also important for modulating SNF responses to N enrichment, with the standardized coefficient being 0.29 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). The N enrichment rate explained 11.7% of the relative importance in SNF responses with a standardized coefficient of −0.30 (p < 0.001) (Fig. 3). The remaining variables (i.e., mean annual temperature and microbial traits) collectively accounted for 24.6% of the relative importance in SNF responses (Fig. 3). Moreover, environmental factors indirectly mediated SNF responses upon N enrichment through plant performance trait modification, with a standardized coefficient of −0.56 for mean annual temperature (p < 0.001), 0.11 for N enrichment rate (p < 0.05), 0.41 for soil carbon:N ratio (p < 0.001), and 0.60 for microbial traits (p < 0.001), respectively (Fig. 3b).
